topics.title: Detritus
topics.text: In biology, detritus is non-living particules of organic origin.  Typically, it includes the bodies or fragments of dead organisms as well as faecal material.

topics.title: Direct development
topics.text: Direct development is an idea in biology.  An animal does direct development if the baby animal looks like a small adult and not a larva.

topics.title: Extant
topics.text: In biology, an extant group is one which has survived to the present day, and so it is a living group. This distinguishes it from an extinct group.

topics.title: Field research
topics.text: Field research is research done in natural surroundings. It is used in biology to contrast with research done in the laboratory.

topics.title: Flora and fauna of Brazil
topics.text: Brazil is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world. Brazil is home to many hummingbirds, toucans, parrots, macaws, waterfowl and birds of prey.

topics.title: Flora and fauna of Mexico
topics.text: Plant and animal life differs sharply with Mexico's varied climate and topography. The coastal plains are covered with a tropical rain forest, which merges into subtropical and temperate growth as the plateau is ascended.

topics.title: Freshwater Biological Association
topics.text: The Freshwater Biological Association, often shortened to the FBA, is a British charity started in 1929. It  aims are  to promote freshwater biology.

topics.title: Function (biology)
topics.text: Function in biology is what a part of the body or cell does in relation to the whole. It is the reason some part or process occurred in a system which evolved by natural selection.

topics.title: Gerontology Research Group
topics.text: Gerontology Research Group is a non profit research group that researches about aging, mainly focusing on people who are 110 years old or older. The group later eventually wants to start slowing and reversing aging.

topics.title: Habit (biology)
topics.text: Habit in biology is about the shape or behaviour of animals and plants.

topics.title: Heracleum sphondylium
topics.text: Heracleum sphondylium commonly called Common hogweed or Cow parsnip is a herbaceous plant in the family Apiaceae native to Europe and Asia.

topics.title: Hermaphrodite
topics.text: Hermaphrodite is a term which comes from Hermaphroditus, the son of Hermes and Aphrodite. It is used as a scientific term in biology.

topics.title: History of biology
topics.text: The history of biology covers the study of the living world from ancient to modern times. People began to think about biology as a specific field in the 1800s.

topics.title: Homology
topics.text: A homologous trait is any characteristic which is derived by evolution from a common ancestor. This is contrasted to analogous traits: similarities between organisms that were evolved separately.

topics.title: Host (biology)
topics.text: A host is an organism which provides shelter for parasites. Parasites will live on the animal and may lay their eggs on them.

topics.title: Hyperossification
topics.text: Hyperossification is when there is much more bone material on a bone than usual.  Hyperossification is found in frogs.

topics.title: International Biology Olympiad
topics.text: The International Biology Olympiad (IBO) is the world's premier biology competition for secondary school students. It is one of the International Science Olympiads.

topics.title: Invasion
topics.text: Invasion is a word that comes from Latin. Originally, it meant that something goes in (as in military occupation) of a foreign territory.

topics.title: Joule
topics.text: The joule (symbol: J) ( or sometimes ) is a unit in the SI system named after English physicist James Prescott Joule.

topics.title: Abstraction (chemistry)
topics.text: In chemistry, abstraction is when one molecule or ion takes an atom from another one. The atom may or may not have electric charge.

topics.title: Acid dissociation constant
topics.text:
The acid dissociation constant is a number that measures the strength of an acid. The constant is written as 
  
    
      
        
          K
          
            a
          
        
      
    
    {\displaystyle K_{a}}
  
, and its negative logarithm as 
  
    
      
        
          p
        
        
          K
          
            a
          
        
      
    
    {\displaystyle \mathrm {p} K_{a}}
  
.

topics.title: Additive
topics.text: In chemistry, an additive is a substance that is added to a mixture or compound to change the properties of that mixture or compound. Food additives are used to improve food.

topics.title: Alkali
topics.text:
In chemistry, an alkali is an aqueous (from water) solution with a pH value of more than seven.
The word 'alkali' comes from the Arabic 'qali' meaning 'from the ashes' since ashes mixed with water used as cleaning products (such as soaps) are made of alkali materials.

topics.title: Allotropy
topics.text: Allotropy (or allotropism) is when a chemical element can exist in two or more different forms in the same physical state or phase. These different forms are called allotropes.

topics.title: Amount of substance
topics.text: Amount of substance (also called chemical amount) is a quantity defined by standards to measure the size a group of individual elementary entities, such as atoms, molecules and electrons, along with other particles. The International System of Units (SI) defines the amount of substance to be equal to the number of elementary entities present.

topics.title: Aqueous solution
topics.text: An aqueous solution is a solution where the solvent is water. In a chemical equation it is written by adding (aq) to the formula.

topics.title: Arrhenius acid-base theory
topics.text: The Arrhenius acid-base theory is the first modern scientific definition of acids and bases. It was discovered by and named after Svante Arrhenius, and was part of why he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903.

topics.title: Atom
topics.text: An atom is an extremely small piece of matter. All normal matter – everything that has mass – is made of atoms.

topics.title: Atomic mass
topics.text: An atomic mass (symbol: ma) is the mass of a single atom of a chemical element. It includes the masses of the 3 subatomic particles that make up an atom: protons, neutrons and electrons.

topics.title: Atomic number
topics.text: The atomic number (symbol: Z) of an atom is the number of protons in the nucleus of the atom. The atomic number of an atom identifies which element it is.

topics.title: Atomic theory
topics.text: In chemistry and physics, the atomic theory explains how our understanding of the atom has changed over time. Atoms were once thought to be the smallest pieces of matter.

topics.title: Base (chemistry)
topics.text: A base is a substance that can accept a hydrogen ion (H+) from another substance. A chemical can accept a proton if it has a negative charge, or if the molecule has an electronegative atom like oxygen, nitrogen, or chlorine that is rich in electrons.

topics.title: Beta particle
topics.text: Beta particles are electrons or positrons emitted by some radioactive nuclei such as potassium-40 or carbon-14 (which becomes nitrogen-14). The beta particles emitted are a form of ionizing radiation sometimes called beta rays.

topics.title: Binary solution
topics.text: A binary solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more than two substances whose composition can change within a certain limits.

topics.title: Bioorthogonal chemistry
topics.text: The term bioorthogonal chemistry is about any chemical reaction that can happen inside of living systems without causing any problems with its native biochemical processes. The term was created by Carolyn Bertozzi in 2003.

topics.title: Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory
topics.text: The Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory (also called proton theory of acids and bases) is one of the two main definitions of acids and bases in modern chemistry, alongside the Lewis acid-base theory. Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted and Thomas Martin Lowry developed the theory in 1923.

topics.title: Chemical energy
topics.text: Chemical energy is the energy produced in a chemical reaction in the form of heat. Using Hess's law it is possible to calculate the amount of energy an exothermic reaction produces.

topics.title: Chemical industry
topics.text: The chemical industry changes raw materials (oil, natural gas, air, water, metals, and minerals) into more than 70,000 different products.  Some chemical companies produce plastics as well as chemicals.

topics.title: Chemical law
topics.text: Chemical laws are the natural, unbreakable laws used in chemistry. The basic idea in chemistry is the law of conservation of mass.

topics.title: Condensed structual formula
topics.text: A condensed structual formula is a mixture of the ease found in the molecular formula, and the information found in the dashed structural formula. In this style, the atoms are usually written without any sort of dashes or other signs, and the hydrogen atoms are written on the right side of the atom connection.

topics.title: Conjugate acids and bases
topics.text:
In chemistry, specifically Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory, an acid and base are conjugates if they can change into each other by adding or removing a hydrogen ion.
An acid-base reaction is a reaction where an acid and a base are converted into their conjugate base and conjugate acid: deprotonation of the acid and protonation of the base.

topics.title: Cooling curve
topics.text: A cooling curve is a line graph that shows how the temperature of a substance changes over time while it cools down. It is often used to study how a material changes from a liquid to a solid, and from a gas to a liquid.

topics.title: Crystal
topics.text:
A crystal is a solid whose atoms (or molecules) are arranged in a repeating pattern. 
Crystals are made from fluids by Crystallization, which is a kind of phase change.

topics.title: Dalton (unit)
topics.text: The dalton or unified atomic mass unit (symbol: Da, amu or u) is a unit of measurement for measuring the mass of atoms, equalling ¹⁄₁₂ of the mass of the carbon-12 isotope, the most abundant form of carbon atoms in nature.

topics.title: Dancing molecule
topics.text: Dancing molecules are moving molecules used in experimental therapy to reverse paralysis and repair tissue after severe spinal cord injuries. Nanoparticles are injected into a victim's body near the spinal cord.

topics.title: Dashed structural formula
topics.text: A dashed structural formula uses straight lines to show chemical bonds. The connections are usually drawn in 90 degree angles or 180 degree angles due to its ease.

topics.title: Deposition (chemistry)
topics.text:
In chemistry, deposition takes place when molecules settle out of a solution.
See also precipitation.

topics.title: Derivative (chemistry)
topics.text: In chemistry, a derivative is a chemical compound related to a different, usually simpler, compound called its parent compound. The term has different meanings in specific contexts, but normally refers to a chemical that is made by replacing a small part of the parent without making big changes to its shape or structure.

topics.title: Desiccant
topics.text: A desiccant, drying agent or dehydrating agent is a substance that is (good at or) effective at removing water; "desiccate" means "make very dry". Many types of desiccants exist, and are used for different purposes.

topics.title: Diatomic molecules
topics.text:
Diatomic molecules are molecules made only of two atoms, of either the same or different chemical elements.
Two atoms are bonded together to form a unit known as a diatomic molecule.

topics.title: Dynamic equilibrium
topics.text: A reversible process is said to be in dynamic equilibrium when the forward and reverse processes occur at the same rate, resulting in no observable change in the system.Once dynamic equilibrium is established, the concentrations or partial pressures of all species involved in the process remain constant.

topics.title: Effusion
topics.text: Effusion is a way gases get out through small holes in materials. For instance, one may fill a balloon with helium, and later discover that all of the gas has gotten out.

topics.title: Electrolysis
topics.text: Electrolysis is a scientific way of 'splitting' substances. It means 'electric-splitting'  and involves the separation of substances through an electric current.

topics.title: Electrolysis of water
topics.text: Electrolysis of water is the decomposition of water into oxygen and hydrogen gas. This technique can be used to produce breathable oxygen or hydrogen gas as a fuel source, referred to as hydrogen fuel.

topics.title: Electron affinity
topics.text: Electron affinity is a term used in chemistry.  When a neutral atom gets an electron, the amount of energy that is released by the atom is the electron affinity.

topics.title: Electron configuration
topics.text: An electron configuration is the arrangement of electrons within an atom. The electron configuration describes where the electrons are inside orbitals.

topics.title: Electron crystallography
topics.text:
Electron crystallography is a method to determine the arrangement of atoms in solids using a transmission electron microscope (TEM).
This method works in many cases where X-ray crystallography does not.

topics.title: Enthalpy of atomization
topics.text:
The enthalpy of atomization is the heat change that resulted to the separation or disintegration of all atoms in a chemical substance.
ΔatH or ΔHat., means "Enthalpy of atomization".

topics.title: Enzyme kinetics
topics.text: Enzyme kinetics is a field of chemistry. It describes how fast reactions happen, that involve enzymes.

topics.title: Absolute space and time
topics.text: Absolute space and time  are concepts used by Aristotle and by Newton. They are still used in classical mechanics.

topics.title: Acceleration due to gravity
topics.text: The acceleration which is gained by an object because of gravitational force is called its acceleration due to gravity. Its SI unit is m/s2.

topics.title: History of physics
topics.text: Physics is a part of science that studies matter (what things are made of) and energy (how things move and change). Long ago, people in different cultures talked about these ideas, but they couldn't tell the difference between real causes of natural events and superstitions.

topics.title: Physics
topics.text: Physics is the science of how things move in space and time and how the universe works. It studies matter and forces.

topics.title: Red mercury
topics.text: Red mercury is a term used for a number of substances that are supposed to exist (or that could possibly exist). So far, no such substance has been found.

topics.title: Relative atomic mass
topics.text: A relative atomic mass (also called atomic weight; symbol: Ar) is a measure of how heavy atoms are. It is the ratio of the average mass per atom of an element from a given sample to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

topics.title: Residue (chemistry)
topics.text: In chemistry, residue is what is left behind after preparation, separation, or purification, such as distillation, evaporation, or filtration.

topics.title: Risk and Safety Statements
topics.text: Risk and Safety Statements are codes that show the hazards of certain chemicals. There are certain R (risk) phrases and S (safety) phrases.

topics.title: Saturation (chemistry)
topics.text:
Saturation in chemistry can be

the point at which a solution of a substance can dissolve no more of that substance. This point of maximum concentration, the saturation point, depends on the temperature of the liquid as well as the chemical nature of the substances involved.

topics.title: Scratch and sniff
topics.text: Scratch and sniff refers to paper that produces an odor when it is scratched. It is made so a smell comes out when the surface is scratched.

topics.title: Secondary alcohol
topics.text: A secondary alcohol is when only two carbon atoms are connected to the hydroxyl-containing carbon atom. This allows a compound with a secondary alcohol to have a slightly different chemical formula from a compound with a primary alcohol or tertiary alcohol.

topics.title: Semi-solid
topics.text: A semi-solid is a state of matter. It is a substance that is in between a solid and a liquid.

topics.title: Semiconductor doping
topics.text: In electronics, doping is the process of adding certain chemical elements to a semiconductor in order to change its electrical conductivity. These elements are tiny impurities.

topics.title: Skeletal formula
topics.text: A skeletal formula is a way of drawing a molecule of an organic compound. They are simplified versions of structural formulas that do not show most carbon or hydrogen atoms.

topics.title: Sky
topics.text: The sky is the appearance of the atmosphere around the surface of the planet from our point of view. We see many objects that are actually in space such as the Sun, the Moon, and stars because they are in the sky.

topics.title: Solubility
topics.text:
Solubility is the ability of a substance (the solute), to mix into a liquid (the solvent).
It measures the highest amount of substance mixed into a liquid solvent while they are both at equal amounts.

topics.title: Solution (chemistry)
topics.text: In chemistry, a solution is a homogeneous mixture  of two or more substances.  The substances that are dissolved are called solutes.

topics.title: Solvent
topics.text: A solvent is a substance that becomes a solution by dissolving a solid, liquid, or gaseous solute. A solvent is usually a liquid, but can also be a solid or gas.

topics.title: Spectral line
topics.text: A spectral line is the way scientists can tell one element from another by looking at color.

topics.title: Alice and Bob
topics.text: Alice and Bob are placeholder names which are commonly used to talk about problems. It is used in cryptography, game theory and physics.

topics.title: Analog signal
topics.text:
An analog or analogue signal is any continuous signal. 
The difference from a digital signal is that also very small fluctuations in the signal are meaningful.

topics.title: Apparent weight
topics.text: Apparent weight is the weight that an object seems to have on a scale or when supported by a surface. It is not the same as the actual weight of the object, which is determined by the force of gravity.

topics.title: Big Crunch
topics.text: The Big Crunch is a possible scenario for the ultimate fate of the universe where the expansion of the universe reverses causing it to collapse in to an infinitely small point, possibly followed by a second Big Bang. A majority of evidence states that this is false.

topics.title: Bose-Einstein statistics
topics.text: In statistical mechanics, Bose-Einstein statistics means the statistics of a system where you can not tell the difference between any of the particles, and the particles are bosons. Bosons are fundamental particles like the photon.

topics.title: Brownian motion
topics.text: Brownian motion is the random motion of particles suspended in a medium (a liquid or a gas). The motion is caused by fast-moving atoms or molecules that hit the particles.

topics.title: CP violation
topics.text: CP Violation is the way that nature breaks the laws that say that when you change a system by C symmetry or P symmetry then some descriptions of the system should stay the same before and after the change. The 'violation' is that they don't stay the same and the amounts are not conserved.

topics.title: Carbonation
topics.text: Carbonation is the process of carbon dioxide dissolving in a liquid. For example, carbon dioxide is added to flavored water under pressure to make it "fizz" as a carbonated water soft drink.

topics.title: Center of percussion
topics.text: The center of percussion is the sweet spot in a sword or object that is swung, the centre of percussion is where the resonance in the object is nullified by the object.

topics.title: Charged particle
topics.text: A charged particle, also called an ion, is an atom with a positive or negative charge. This happens whenever something called an ionic bond forms.

topics.title: Classical field theory
topics.text: Classical physics is a group of physics theories that predate modern, more complete, or more widely applicable theories. If a currently accepted theory is considered to be modern, and its introduction represented a major paradigm shift, then the previous theories, or new theories based on the older paradigm, will often be referred to as belonging to the area of "classical physics".

topics.title: Classical physics
topics.text: Classical physics are the physics that were made before the 20th century. This part of physics studies things like movement, light, gravity, and electricity.

topics.title: Clinamen
topics.text: Clinamen is the word Lucretius gave to the unpredictable swerve of atoms. He means that these atoms don't just fall down, but because of the swerve collisions happen.

topics.title: Cloud physics
topics.text: Cloud physics is the study of how clouds are formed in the atmosphere. Clouds can be droplets of water, ice crystals or both, along with dust or smoke particles onto which water or ice can condense.

topics.title: Coefficient of friction
topics.text: A coefficient of friction is a value that shows the relationship between two objects and the normal reaction between the objects that are involved. It is a value that is sometimes used in physics to find an object's normal force or frictional force when other methods are unavailable.

topics.title: Complexity
topics.text: Complexity is a property of an object with many parts and a complicated arrangement. It is also the state of being complex.

topics.title: Conjugate variables
topics.text: Conjugate variables are special pairs of variables (like x, y, z) that don't give the same result when you do a certain mathematical operation with them. This means that x*y is not equal to y*x.

topics.title: Dellinger effect
topics.text: Solar flares are large bursts of energy coming from the sun. On Earth, these flares disrupt radio communication.

topics.title: Dissipation
topics.text: In physics, dissipation includes the concept of a dynamical system where important mechanical modes, such as waves or oscillations, lose energy over time, typically due to the action of friction or turbulence. The lost energy is converted into heat, raising the temperature of the system.

topics.title: Elastic collision
topics.text: An elastic collision is when two objects collide and bounce back with little or no deformation. For example, two rubber balls bouncing together would be elastic.

topics.title: Physical system
topics.text: In physics, a physical system is any object or part of an object that can be analysed with the laws of physics. An atom or the water in a lake can both be considered as physical systems.

topics.title: Platonic crystal
topics.text:
Platonic crystals are periodic structures which are designed to guide flexural wave energy through thin elastic plates.
The study of platonic crystals is referred to as platonics and does not refer to the teachings of Plato or the Platonic solids.

topics.title: Polarity
topics.text:
In physics, polarity describes an attribute that can usually have two values:

An electric charge has a polarity of either positive or negative.
A voltage has a polarity, in that it could be positive or negative (with respect to some other voltage, such as the one at the other end of a battery or electric circuit).

topics.title: Positronium
topics.text: Positronium is an onium, a type of exotic atom that is made of a particle and its antiparticle. In Positronium, one positron and one electron are bonded together.

topics.title: QED vacuum
topics.text: QED vacuum is the vacuum explained by quantum electrodynamics. In this theory, a vacuum is not fully empty.

topics.title: Quantum gravity
topics.text: Quantum gravity is an area of research in physics. Right now, physics can describe gravity of real-life-sized objects using general relativity.

topics.title: Radioactive contamination
topics.text: Radioactive contamination  or radiological contamination is the contamination of the environment with radioactive materials, where these materials are not present. Many radioactive substances have very long half lives; this means that if they are present in the envioroment, they can be dangerous for a very long time.

topics.title: Rayleigh scattering
topics.text: Rayleigh scattering is the way that light scatters when it hits a very small object.  This theory is valid if the wavelength of the light is much bigger than the object.

topics.title: Reduced mass
topics.text: Reduced mass is an idea from physics. The two-body problem is a problem of two bodies influencing each other.

topics.title: Resonance
topics.text: In physics, resonance is the tendency of a system to vibrate with increasing amplitudes at some frequencies of excitation. These are known as the system's resonant frequencies (or resonance frequencies).

topics.title: Resonator
topics.text: A resonator is something that resonates.  This may make a particular frequency of a sound or other vibration become bigger.

topics.title: Resultant force
topics.text:
A resultant force, also called a net force, is a force equal to the sum of all forces applied to an object.
If 30N and 60N are applied to the right, then the resultant force is 90N to the right.

topics.title: Rigidly rotating disk paradox
topics.text: In theoretical physics, a branch of physics, the rigidly rotating disk paradox, sometimes called the Ehrenfest paradox, is a paradox concerning a rotating disk. Basically, the paradox says that when a disk (or any circular object in general) is rotated, it will have a smaller circumference than 2πr, because the radius will remain the same, but the circumference is shortened due to the Lorentz contraction.

topics.title: Rutherford scattering
topics.text: Rutherford scattering is the elastic scattering of charged particles. This is caused by the Coulomb interaction.

topics.title: Schumann resonances
topics.text: A Schumann resonance is a resonant frequency of a set of several Extremely Low Frequency (ELF) oscillations of the Earth's electromagnetic field between the ground and reflective regions of the ionosphere, triggered by lightning.

topics.title: Separation process
topics.text: Separation processes are methods used in science and engineering to break mixtures apart into their individual parts. These methods work by taking advantage of the differences in physical or chemical properties like size, weight, boiling point, or how something dissolves.

topics.title: Shear modulus
topics.text: Shear modulus is a measure of the amount of force that will shear or twist an object. It is normally the letter G

topics.title: Simple machine
topics.text: A simple machine is a device that can change the direction or the magnitude of a force, or the point where it is applied. This is done so that the force can be used to do work.

topics.title: Skyrmion
topics.text: A skyrmion is a quantum entity in atomic physics that can occur in some materials like solids and Bose–Einstein condensates. They are made up from a persistent vortex that is a quantum superposition of baryons and resonance states.

topics.title: Sorption
topics.text: When two chemical substances come in contact with each other, through what is called a phase, they will interact with each other in that phase. They may also have an  interface.

topics.title: Fields Medal
topics.text: The Fields Medal is a prize given to mathematicians who are not over 40 years of age. It is given at each International Congress of the International Mathematical Union.

topics.title: Finity
topics.text: Finity is the opposite of infinity. It is the state of being finite.

topics.title: Fixed-point arithmetic
topics.text: In mathematics, a fixed point is a value that remains unchanged under the application of a given function. Formally, for a function f mapping a set to itself, a fixed point is an element x such that f(x) = x.

topics.title: Fixed point
topics.text: A value x is a fixed point of a function f if and only if f(x) = x.

topics.title: Floating point
topics.text: Real numbers in binary have to be stored in a special way in a computer. Computers represent numbers as binary integers (whole numbers that are powers of two), so there is no direct way for them to represent non-integer numbers like decimals as there is no radix point.

topics.title: Flux
topics.text: Flux is a term in physics and mathematics. It is broadly defined as "How much stuff goes through a thing" (or into an area).

topics.title: Formal language
topics.text:
In mathematics, computer science and linguistics, a formal language is one that has a particular set of symbols, and whose expressions are made according to a particular set of rules. The symbol 
  
    
      
        
          
            L
          
        
      
    
    {\displaystyle {\mathcal {L}}}
  
 is often used as a variable for formal languages in logic.

topics.title: Formal verification
topics.text: Formal verification is the process used to prove that a piece of software or hardware works according to its specification. Formal verification uses a mathematical proof.

topics.title: Function composition
topics.text:
In mathematics, function composition is a way of making a new function from two other functions through a chain-like process.
More specifically, given a function f  from X to Y and a function g from Y to Z, then the function "g composed with f", written as g ∘ f, is a function from X to Z (notice how it is usually written in the opposite way to how people would expect it to be).

topics.title: Function space
topics.text: In mathematics, a function space is a set of functions of a given kind from a set X to a set Y. For example:

topics.title: General topology
topics.text: General topology is a branch of topology. It uses set theory to model topological porblems.

topics.title: Generalization (mathematics)
topics.text:
In mathematics, generalization is the idea of taking some of the properties of some physical or mathematical object and examining just those specific properties, without relying on other things about the objects they came from.
Generalization is an important mathematical tool because it allows for statements to be made about large groups of mathematical objects at once.

topics.title: Golden spiral
topics.text: The Golden Spiral is a part of Math, which is shown in Fibonacci’s Model.

topics.title: Graph
topics.text: A graph is a picture designed to express words, particularly the connection between two or more quantities. You can see a graph on the right.

topics.title: Heaviside function
topics.text:
The Heaviside function, often written as H(x), is a non-continuous function whose value is zero for a negative input and one for a positive input.
The function is used in the mathematics of control theory to represent a signal that switches on at a specified time, and which stays switched on indefinitely.

topics.title: Heuristic
topics.text: A heuristic is a practical way to solve a problem. It is better than chance, but does not always work.

topics.title: Horizontal
topics.text: Horizontal is a direction perpendicular to the vertical. That is, it goes in all directions except up and down.

topics.title: Hyperplane arrangements
topics.text: Hyperplane arrangements is a branch of mathematics that studies how smaller objects, called hyperplanes, can be arranged in a bigger object. This is related to other fields of mathematics like number theory, combinatorics, and topology.

topics.title: Idempotence
topics.text: Idempotence is a property that an operation in mathematics or computer science may have. It roughly means that the operation can be carried out again and again without changing the result.

topics.title: Indeterminate form
topics.text: In calculus, an indeterminate form is an expression that has no single solution. There may be no solution, only one, or multiple depending on how the problem is looked at.

topics.title: Maximum and minimum
Mental abacus
topics.text: The mental abacus system is a way to calculate math in your head, by imagining an abacus. People can calculate math very fast this way.

topics.title: Mental calculation
topics.text: Mental calculation or mental maths is doing arithmetic without using any tools such as a computer or a calculator. and without writing anything down.

topics.title: Mental calculator
topics.text: A mental calculator is primarily a person who can perform mathematical calculations in their mind. It is also known as mental arithmetic, mental calculation, quick math, fast math, or doing math in your head.

topics.title: Methods of computing square roots
topics.text:
The square root of a number 
  
    
      
        n
      
    
    {\displaystyle n}
  
 is whatever number equals 
  
    
      
        n
      
    
    {\displaystyle n}
  
 when multiplied by itself (squared). There are many ways to calculate square roots, from estimations to precise calculations.

topics.title: Millennium Prize Problems
topics.text: The Millennium Problems are a set of seven unsolved mathematical problems designated by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. These challenges cover a wide range of mathematical disciplines, from number theory to Topology, and solving any one of them would earn the solver a $1 million prize.

topics.title: Module (mathematics)
topics.text: In abstract algebra, a module is the generalization of a vector space. Modules are defined with respect to a ring.

topics.title: Moiré pattern
topics.text: A moiré pattern is a type of pattern that appears when two similar patterns are overlaid on top of each other. The overlapping creates a new pattern that can be different from the original patterns.

topics.title: Möbius function
topics.text: The Möbius function is the function µ(x,d,g,f,h,c)=mod(|(x^(sqrt(n))-sin(f^(1/g)))/ln(h^c)|,1). It is commonly used in generating a random irrational number.

topics.title: Names of large numbers
topics.text: There are two main ways of using words to write large numbers. The American way or "short form" for naming large numbers is different from the European way or "long form" of naming large numbers.

topics.title: New Math
topics.text: New Mathematics or New Math was a change in the way mathematics was taught in schools. It happened between the 1950s, and 1970s.

topics.title: Nonlinear programming
topics.text: Nonlinear programming is a way to solve a mathematical optimization problem. A number of equations and inequalities defines such a system.

topics.title: Nth root
topics.text: An n-th root of a number r is a number which, if n copies are multiplied together, makes r. It is also called a radical or a radical expression.

topics.title: Number line
topics.text: A number line is a line with integers (simply ordinary numbers, ...-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3...) on it extending forever in both directions. Usually, zero (0) is placed in the middle of the line.

topics.title: Number of the Beast
topics.text: The number of the Beast (from Ancient Greek: ἑξακόσιοι ἑξήκοντα ἕξ, romanized: hexakósioi hexēkonta héx, lit. 'six hundred sixty-six') is the fear of the number 666. It comes from the Biblical verse Revelation 13:18, which says that the number 666 is the number of the beast, associated with Satan or the Antichrist.

topics.title: Numerical digit
topics.text: Numerical digits are the number text characters used to show numerals. For example, the numeral "56" has two digits: 5 and 6.

topics.title: On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences
topics.text: The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), also known as Sloane's, is a large searchable database. It is on the Web, and it contains number sequences, like the Fibonacci numbers or the powers of two.

topics.title: Operand
topics.text: In mathematics, an operand is a number or variable being worked on in an equation or inequality.

topics.title: Operation (mathematics)
topics.text: In mathematics, an operation is a function which takes one or more inputs (named operands) and produces an output. Common operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, all of which take two inputs and produce an output.

topics.title: Operator
3D projection
topics.text:
A 3D projection is a way of showing a three-dimensional environment on a two-dimensional flat surface or screen.
A projection is usually calculated using complex mathematical equations.

topics.title: 4D
topics.text: 4D, meaning the common 4 dimensions, is a theoretical concept in mathematics. It has been studied by mathematicians and philosophers since the 18th century.

topics.title: Adjacent
topics.text:
Adjacent is an adjective meaning next to.
In geometry, two sides that meet to create an angle are said to be adjacent.

topics.title: Affine symmetric group
topics.text: Flat, straight-edged shapes (like triangles) or 3D ones (like pyramids) have only a finite number of symmetries - ways to reflect or rotate it where it looks the same. In contrast, the affine symmetric group is a way to mathematically describe all the symmetries possible when an infinitely large flat surface is covered by triangular tiles.

topics.title: Alternate interior angles
topics.text: Alternate interior angles are a concept in geometry that happens when two straight lines are crossed by a third line called a transversal. When this happens, many small angles are formed at the points where the lines meet.

topics.title: Angle bisector
topics.text: Angle bisector is Line or segment that divides an angle into two equal parts. This means it splits one angle into two smaller angles that have the same measure.

topics.title: Apothem
topics.text: The apothem (sometimes shortened to apo) of a regular polygon is a line segment from the center of the polygon to the middle of one of its sides. It is also perpendicular to that side.

topics.title: Arc
topics.text: An arc is a part of a circle. An arc is a curved line.

topics.title: Area
topics.text: Area is the amount of space a two dimensional (flat) surface takes up. It is useful because it is how much of a material is needed to make a hollow container.

topics.title: Axis of rotation
topics.text: The axis of rotation is an imaginary line passing through the center of mass of any celestial body around which the celestial body rotates. In case of Earth, the axis of rotation of Earth passes through the north pole, the centre of mass of Earth and the south pole.

topics.title: Base (geometry)
topics.text:
In plane geometry, the base is the side on which a polygon rests on, and which is used as a referenced side for other measurements. The base of a triangle or quadrilateral is often written as 
  
    
      
        b
      
    
    {\displaystyle b}
  
.

topics.title: Bisection
topics.text: In geometry, bisection is the division of something into two equal parts. This is usually done by a line, which we will call the "bisector".

topics.title: Catenary
topics.text: A catenary is a type of curve. An ideal chain hanging between two supports and acted on by a uniform gravitational force makes the shape of a catenary.

topics.title: Centroid
topics.text: The centroid of a triangle is where all of the medians of a triangle meet. A median is measured from the midpoint of one of the sides, to the vertex opposite to the side.

topics.title: Chord (math)
topics.text: The chord is a term used in geometry to describe a segment that is connected to a curve. It is defined a lot as a segment whose endpoints lie on a circle.

topics.title: Circumference
topics.text: In geometry, circumference is the distance around a closed curve; for example, a circle. It is a special kind of perimeter.

topics.title: Concentric
topics.text: Concentric objects share the same center, axis, or origin. Circles, spheres, cylinders, tubes, and other round objects can be concentric.

More formally, two sets of points are called congruent, if and only if one can be transformed into the other by isometry.

topics.title: Convex set
topics.text: In Euclidean space, a region is a convex set if the following is true. For any two points inside the region, a straight line segment can be drawn.

topics.title: Anangpal Tomar
topics.text: Anangpal Tomar or Anangpal Tanwar (also known as Anangpal II) was a Rajput ruler from the Tomara dynasty. He is known to have established and populated Delhi in the 11th century.

topics.title: Antisemitism
topics.text: Antisemitism is the bias, prejudice or discrimination against Jews. A synonym of antisemitism is Judeophobia, preferred by those considering "antisemitism" ambiguous.

topics.title: Auxiliary sciences of history
topics.text:
The auxiliary sciences of history are fields of study based on historical sources and items. 
Many of those fields of study started between the 16th and 19th centuries.

topics.title: Civilization
topics.text: Civilization (or civilisation) comes from the Latin word civis meaning someone who lives in a city. The Romans usually wanted conquered people to live in towns.

topics.title: Diplomatics
topics.text: Diplomatics is a discipline which is concerned with the analysis of historical documents. The word goes back to diploma, which literally means folded (document).

topics.title: Disinformation
topics.text: Disinformation refers to false information spread intentionally to make a targeted audience believe something that is not based on facts. Disinformation may include the distribution of forged documents, manuscripts and photographs, or the promotion of harmful rumors, conspiracy theories and fake intelligence.

topics.title: Emancipation
topics.text: Emancipation is any time when someone tries to have more economic and social rights, political rights or equality. This is usually for a group of people that feels disfranchised.

topics.title: Genocide
topics.text: During a genocide, a group (often a government, army, or paramilitary) tries to destroy another group because of their ethnicity, race, nationality or religion. Genocide is always an intentional act - never an accident.

topics.title: Guillotine
topics.text:
The guillotine is a machine used to execute people by decapitation (chopping off their heads). 
A guillotine is made of a heavy blade attached to a rack, which moves up and down on a vertical frame.

topics.title: Historical method
topics.text: The historical method are the techniques and guidelines by which historians use primary sources and other evidence to research and then to write history.

topics.title: Historical source
topics.text: A historical source is an original document or item that holds important information about the past. These sources are fundamental for understanding history and serve as clues for historical study.

topics.title: Historicism
topics.text: Historicism is an approach to explaining the existence of phenomena, especially social and cultural practices (including ideas and beliefs), by studying their history, that is, by studying the process through which they arose. The term is widely used in philosophy, anthropology, and sociology.

topics.title: History
topics.text: History is the study of past events. People know what happened in the past by looking at things from the past including sources (like books, newspapers, scripts and letters), buildings and different types of artifacts (like pottery, tools, coins and human or animal remains.) Libraries, archives, and museums collect and keep these things for people to study history.

topics.title: History of agriculture
topics.text: Agriculture is the activity of growing crops and raising animals for food, clothing and other products. Farmers grow certain plants and raise certain animals depending on their environment.

topics.title: Human history
topics.text: Human history is the study of the human race from prehistory to the present day. It is part of natural history.

topics.title: Near East
topics.text: The Near East is a large area of land in the eastern hemisphere. Countries of the eastern Mediterranean are part of the Near East.

topics.title: Old Style and New Style dates
topics.text: Old Style (or O.S.) and New Style (or N.S.) are terms used for calendar dates in English language historical studies, for two reasons. The first reason is that the method of dating that is most widely used around the world today, the Gregorian calendar, was introduced into English cultures only in 1752.

topics.title: Oral history
topics.text: Oral history is history that is told rather than written down. It is given through talking rather than reading a book.

topics.title: Sphere packing
topics.text: In geometry, Sphere packing refers to a number of problems that try to arrange spheres in space. Very often, the spheres all have the same size, and the space used is usually three-dimensional Euclidean space.

topics.title: Squaring the circle
topics.text: Squaring the circle is a problem of geometry. The problem is to construct a square that has the same area as the unit circle, only by using a compass and straightedge construction method.

topics.title: Agile ground mantis
topics.text: The agile ground mantis (Litaneutria minor) is a species of Mantodea in the family Mantidae. It is native to the United States and small parts of Canada.

topics.title: Air space
topics.text: Air space is the area of the air that is controlled by a country or organisation. You have to have the permission of the controller to enter their air space in an airplane.

topics.title: Amphibian
topics.text: Amphibians are members of the class Amphibia. The living ones are frogs (including toads), salamanders (including newts) and caecilians.

topics.title: Animal
topics.text:
Animals (or Metazoa) are living creatures with many cells that make up the kingdom Animalia. 
Animals get their energy from other living things.

topics.title: Arthropod
topics.text: Arthropods (Greek language for "joint-legged") are a large group of invertebrate animals. Insects, spiders, crabs, shrimp, millipedes, and centipedes are all arthropods.

topics.title: Bilateria
topics.text: The Bilateria are animals which are bilaterally symmetrical. They have front and a back end, an upside and downside, and a left and right side.

topics.title: Chordate
topics.text: Chordates, phylum Chordata, are a phylum of animals which have a notochord. The group includes vertebrates, with some closely related invertebrates.

topics.title: Decimal degrees
topics.text:
Decimal degrees are the latitude and longitude geographic coordinates as decimal fractions.
Positive latitudes are north of the equator and less than zero latitudes are south of equator.

topics.title: Deuterostome
topics.text: Deuterostomes are a nephrozoan superphylum of bilaterian animals, a taxon above the level of phylum. It is not part of the usual system of classification.

topics.title: Earthworm
topics.text: An earthworm is an invertebrate animal with a long, stretchy body and no legs. It is a type of annelid worm.

topics.title: Ecdysozoa
topics.text: The Ecdysozoa (including Cycloneuralia) are a group of protostome animal phyla. This is a taxon above the level of phylum.

topics.title: Geographical renaming
topics.text:
Geographical renaming is when a place's name gets changed. 
There can be several reasons for geographical renaming.

topics.title: Geography
topics.text: Geography (from Greek: γεωγραφία, geographia, literally  "earth description") is the study of earth and its people. It is one of the social sciences.

topics.title: Ground
topics.text: Ground is a common word for the surface of the Earth. It is dirt and rocks that we walk on.

topics.title: International Festival of Geography
topics.text: The International Geography Festival is an event held every year by the Association for the Development of FIG (ADFIG). It is related to geography.

topics.title: International Geographical Union
topics.text: The International Geographical Union (IGU; French: Union Géographique Internationale, UGI) is an international association of geographical organizations around the world. The organization was established in 1922 in Belgium after the first geographical congress, which was in 1871.

topics.title: Land
topics.text: Land can mean some territory, forming part of a country. Dry land is the parts of Earth's surface not covered by the ocean or other permanent body of water.

topics.title: Land reclamation
topics.text: Land reclamation is the idea of getting new land. It is usually done in coastal areas.

topics.title: Landmarks
topics.text:
Originally, a landmark literally meant a prominent, easily identified geographic point, (like a mountain, a cliff, or a river) used by explorers and others to find their way back or through an area.
In modern use, it includes anything that can be recognized easily, such as a monument, building, or other structure.

topics.title: Landscape
topics.text: A landscape means an area of land as one can see it. This includes landforms, flora, fauna and human elements, for instance human activity or the built environment.

topics.title: Aardvark
topics.text: The aardvark (Orycteropus afer) is a mammal from Africa; its name means "earth pig" in the language Afrikaans.

topics.title: Afrosoricida
topics.text: Afrosoricida is an order of mammals, which includes the Tenrecs and the Golden mole. Tenrecs look like hedgehogs in appearance.

topics.title: Afrotheria
topics.text: The Afrotheria is a group of mammals, (a superorder or a clade). It includes the golden moles, elephant shrews, tenrecs, aardvarks, hyraxes, elephants and manatees.

topics.title: Alpine ibex
topics.text: The Alpine ibex (Capra ibex) is a species of wild goat. It lives in the mountains of the European Alps.

topics.title: Archonta
topics.text: The Archonta is a deprecated superorder of placental mammals, in which are included bats, primates, colugos, and treeshrews.

topics.title: Arsinoitherium
topics.text: Arsinoitherium is an extinct genus, a large mammal that lived during the early Oligocene (about 38 to 23 million years ago). Although it looked like a rhinoceros, it is more closely related to elephants.

topics.title: Artiodactyl
topics.text: The Artiodactyla are even-toed ungulates, an order of mammals. They have an even number of toes: two or four.

topics.title: Bat
topics.text: Bats are mammals in the order Chiroptera. Bats are nocturnal which means they are active during the night, dusk, or dawn and they sleep at day.

topics.title: Boreoeutheria
topics.text: Boreoeutheria (also Boreotheria) are mammals that are the third superorder of placental mammals. The other two groups are Afrotheria and Xenarthra.

topics.title: Brindle
topics.text: Brindle is a fur coloring in animals. It mainly appears on dogs, cats, cattle, and sometimes horses.

topics.title: Carnassial
topics.text:
Carnassials are large teeth used for shearing flesh and bone in a scissor- or shear-like way. They are found in many carnivorous mammals, 
In the Carnivora, the carnassials are the modified last upper premolar and the first molar.

topics.title: Cetartiodactyla
topics.text: Cetartiodactyla is a proposed taxonomical superorder which includes whales (and dolphins) and even-toed ungulates.  The name was created by merging the name for the two orders, Cetacea and Artiodactyla, into a single word.

topics.title: Eumetazoa
topics.text: Eumetazoa is a clade which includes all major animal phyla except for sponges, and a few other groups of animals, such as the Placozoa. The Eumetazoa have true tissues, neurons, and an embryo that goes through a gastrula stage.

topics.title: Feral
topics.text:
A feral organism is a plant or animal which has changed from being tame or cultivated to being wild. 
A feral animal is one which has escaped from a domestic or captive status and is living more or less as a wild animal.

topics.title: Fish
topics.text: Fish (plural: fish or fishes) are a group of animals which live in water and respire (get oxygen) from their gills. As a group, they are much older than other vertebrates.

topics.title: Gnathostomata
topics.text:
Gnathostomata is the group of vertebrates with jaws.
The group was meant to include all jawed fish, but in modern fashion it also includes all the tetrapods as well, since they evolved from jawed fish.

topics.title: Hemipristis
topics.text: Hemipristis is a genus of weasel shark that lived in Late Jurassic to recent. It contains one living species: Weasel Shark (Hemipristis elongata).

topics.title: Holocene extinction
topics.text: The Holocene extinction is the extinction of nearly all large mammal species after the end of the ice age. This was done by humans hunting the animals, and by climate change.

topics.title: Insect
topics.text: Insects are a class in the phylum Arthropoda. They are small terrestrial invertebrates which have a hard exoskeleton.

topics.title: Invertebrate
topics.text: An invertebrate is an animal that does not have a spine or backbone. This contrasts with vertebrate: if an animal is not a vertebrate (fish, reptile, amphibian, bird, or mammal), it is an invertebrate.

topics.title: Cladotheria
topics.text: Cladotheria is a taxonomic group. It includes two of the three living groups of mammals.

topics.title: Dental formula
topics.text:
A dental formula is a summary of a mammal's teeth.
Almost all mammals have four kinds of teeth:

incisors
canines
premolars
molars
Teeth numbers and form have adapted to different feeding methods.

topics.title: Elephant shrew
topics.text: The elephant shrews, also called sengis, are any of 16 species of rat-sized African mammals named for their long, tapered, and flexible snout (proboscis).  All have slim bodies, slender limbs, and very long hind legs and feet.

topics.title: Embrithopoda
topics.text: Embrithopoda ("heavy-footed") is an order of extinct mammals from Asia, Africa and Eastern Europe.

topics.title: Euarchonta
topics.text:
The Euarchonta are a grandorder of mammals containing four orders: the Dermoptera or colugos, the Scandentia or treeshrews, the extinct Plesiadapiformes, and the Primates.
Euarchonta and Glires together form the Euarchontoglires, one of the four Eutherian clades.

topics.title: Euarchontoglires
topics.text: Euarchontoglires (synonymous with Supraprimates) is a taxonomic superorder, within Placentalia. It includes the rodents and the primates.

topics.title: Eutheria
topics.text:
Eutheria is the taxonomical name for the main group of living mammals.
This taxon contains the placental mammals, of which humans are one species.

topics.title: Ferae
topics.text: Ferae (meaning wild beasts) is a mirorder in Ferungulata for multiple groups of mammals that carry babies in the uterus. It includes Carnivora and its fossil relatives, pangolins and its fossil relatives, and the extinct Pantalesta.

topics.title: Ferungulata
topics.text: Ferungulata is a group of mammals containing pholidota, carnivora, ungulata, and their extinct relatives. Ferungulata is a sister group to chiroptera, the bats, together these two groups create the clade scrotifera.

topics.title: Fur
topics.text:
Fur is the hair of mammals. Different species may have quite different styles of hair, making them more or less suitable to the fur trade, but many are as follows:
Fur usually consists of two main layers:

Down hair (known also as undercoat or ground hair) — the bottom layer.

topics.title: Glires
topics.text: Glires (from Latin glīrēs, dormice) is a clade (sometimes ranked as grandorder) consisting of rodents and lagomorphs (rabbits, hares, and pikas). This hypothesis that these form a monophyletic group has been long debated based on morphological evidence, although recent morphological studies strongly support monophyly of Glires.

topics.title: Hippopotamus
topics.text: The hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius), or hippo, ancient Greek for "river horse" (Ιπποπόταμος), also known as the Nile hippopotamus, Common hippopotamus, or River hippopotamus, is a large mammal from Africa that usually eats plants. It is one of only two species in the family Hippopotamidae that are still alive.

topics.title: Incisor
topics.text: Incisors are special kinds of teeth that can be found in some mammals, such as humans. They are the eight large flat  teeth with straight edges that are at the front of a person's mouth, in between the canine teeth, which are pointed.

topics.title: Kvabebihyrax
topics.text:
Kvabebihyrax kachethicus is an extinct hyrax from the Pliocene that lived in the Caucasus region.
With a length of 1.6 metres (5 ft 4 in), Kvabebihyrax was much larger than modern hyraxes, comparable in size to larger species of the Paleogene genus Titanohyrax.

topics.title: Lactation
topics.text: Lactation describes the secretion of milk from the breasts when a mother feeds her young. It occurs with almost all female mammals after the birth of their young.

topics.title: Largest Artiodactyls
topics.text: The following is a list of largest mammals in the even-toed ungulates, that is, the Artiodactyls.

topics.title: Laurasiatheria
topics.text: Laurasiatheria is a large group of placental mammals. The name comes from the area where advanced mammals evolved.

topics.title: Mammal-like reptile
topics.text:
Mammal-like reptile is an old term for the therapsids: those synapsids which gave rise to the true mammals.
The term is both outmoded and a mistake, because mammals did not descend from reptiles.

topics.title: Mammalogy
topics.text:
Mammalogy is the study of the mammals. Mammalogy has also been known as "mastology," "theriology," and "therology." 
Mammals are a group of vertebrate animals.

topics.title: Monotreme
topics.text: Monotremes are a group of mammals that form the order Monotremata. Monotremes are the only mammals that lay eggs, but they also feed their babies with milk.

topics.title: American Ornithologists' Union
topics.text: The American Ornithologists' Union (AOU) is an ornithological organization. It is found in the USA

topics.title: Ant-follower
topics.text: The ant-follower is a bird which feeds by following army ants. They take the prey that the ants have.

topics.title: Anting
topics.text: Anting is a behavior in which birds rub insects (usually ants) on their feathers. This releases liquids with chemicals such as formic acid onto the bird's feathers.

topics.title: Archaeopteryx
topics.text: Archaeopteryx is one of the most important creatures ever discovered. It is a flying dinosaur from the end of the Jurassic Period, about 150 million years ago.

topics.title: Atlantic puffin
topics.text: The Atlantic Puffin, also known as the Common Puffin a type of seabird in the auk family. It spends most of its time on the ocean.

topics.title: Avialae
topics.text: Avialae is a term for birds and their immediate extinct ancestors. It is a clade of dinosaurs containing their only living representatives (birds) and whatever coelurosaurs are regarded as their ancestors.

topics.title: Aviary
topics.text: An aviary is a place where birds are kept. It is larger than a birdcage.

topics.title: Avivore
topics.text: An avivore is an animal that mostly preys on and eats birds. Birds that eats other birds, such as hawks, eagles, and falcons, are called avian avivores.

topics.title: Bird
topics.text: Birds (Aves) are a group of animals with backbones. Birds are the only dinosaurs that survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, and are part of the theropod group of dinosaurs.

topics.title: Bird bath
topics.text: A bird bath is an artificial "puddle" or small shallow pond, created with a water-filled basin, for birds to bathe in, cool off, and drink from. A bird bath can be a garden decoration, small reflecting pool, or outdoor sculpture.

topics.title: Bird cage
topics.text: A bird cage (sometimes birdcage) is a cage to hold a bird. Bird cages are used in the home to contain a pet bird, such as a parakeet or a canary.

topics.title: Bird feet
topics.text: Bird feet are adapted to the life they lead, and the patterns are often use in avian classification. They are derived from the basic limb of ancestral tetrapods, the pentadactyl limb.

topics.title: Bird flight
topics.text: Flight is a method of moving through the air.  To do this, birds use wings with light, hollow bones and feathers on them.

topics.title: Bird nest
topics.text: A bird nest is a place where a bird lays its eggs. There are all kinds of nests, including cup nests, holes in the ground, and piles of twigs and leaves.

topics.title: Bird of prey
topics.text: A bird of prey (also called raptor) is a bird that mainly uses its claws (called talons) to seize prey. They have strong sharp, hooked beaks and claws and have sharp eyesight.

topics.title: Bird sound
topics.text: Bird sounds include bird songs, calls and any other noises they make for communication. Birds do a lot of communicating, mostly to other birds of the same species.

topics.title: Birdbox
topics.text: A birdbox is a human-made, usually wooden box used as a house for birds. It is suitable as a bird home because it is similar to a natural bird home, such as a hollow tree, and birds often make nests inside birdboxes.

topics.title: Birdwatching
topics.text: Birdwatching or birding means going outside to enjoy watching birds. It is a popular hobby.

topics.title: Black-throated loon
topics.text:
The black-throated loon (Gavia arctica), also known as the Arctic loon and the black-throated diver, is a medium-sized member of the loon or diver family, the Gaviidae.
It is a migratory aquatic bird found in the northern hemisphere.

topics.title: Brood parasitism
topics.text: Brood parasites are animals, usually birds, which trick other species to raise their young. The best-known example is the cuckoo.

topics.title: Moorhen
topics.text: A moorhen is a series of birds belonging to the Rallidae species. It is Latin for "little hen" due to its size.

topics.title: Mousebird
topics.text: A mousebird is one of a small group of birds. They are not closely related to other groups of birds.

topics.title: Neoaves
topics.text: Neoaves is a clade. It includes all modern birds (Neornithes or Aves) except Paleognathae (ratites and kin) and Galloanserae (ducks, chickens and kin).

topics.title: Neognathae
topics.text: Neognathae is an infraclass containing almost every single species of bird. Neognathae include almost all living birds: their sister taxon Palaeognathae has just the tinamou and the flightless ratites.

topics.title: Neornithes
topics.text: Neornithes are the most recent common ancestor of all living birds and all their descendants. There are about 9,000 to 10,000 known living species in the world.

topics.title: Nightjar
topics.text: Nightjars are medium-sized birds that are active during the dawn and dusk, or during the night. They can be found all over the world.

topics.title: Origin of birds
topics.text: The origin of birds is one of the most interesting questions in palaeontology and evolution. Birds evolved from theropod dinosaurs during the Mesozoic era.

topics.title: Ornithurae
topics.text: Ornithurae (meaning 'bird tails' in Greek) is the name of a natural group which includes all modern birds as well as their extinct relatives with plough-shaped pygostyles (†Ichthyornis, †Hesperornithes, †Limenavis). This is a bone at the end of the tail which allows the tail feathers to fan and retract.

topics.title: Palaeognathae
topics.text: The Palaeognathae, or paleognaths (from Ancient Greek palaió- "old" + gnáthos "jaw") is one of two living clades of birds: the other is the Neognathae. Together, the two clades make up the clade Neornithes.

topics.title: Paraves
topics.text: Paraves is a branch-based clade containing birds (clade Aves) and other closely related dinosaurs. The paravians include the Avialae, such as Archaeopteryx, and the Deinonychosauria, which includes the dromaeosaurids and troodontids.

topics.title: Passerea
topics.text: Passerea is a clade of birds that was created by Jarvis et al. (2014).

topics.title: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds
topics.text: The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) is an organisation registered in Great Britain as a charity. It was founded as the Plumage League in 1889 by Emily Williamson.

topics.title: Rynchops
topics.text: Skimmers or Rynchops, also called scissorbills, are sea birds in the genus Rynchops. They have a lower jaw that is longer than their upper jaw.

topics.title: Sandgrouse
topics.text: The sandgrouse is any one of the sixteen species of a family of ground-dwelling birds known as the Pteroclidae. They usually occur in steppe-like environments, with large open spaces, and few if any trees.

topics.title: Sibley-Monroe checklist 1
topics.text: The Sibley-Monroe checklist was a landmark document in the study of birds conducted by Charles Sibley and Burt Monroe during the late 1970s and throughout the 1980s. It drew on extensive DNA-DNA hybridisation studies to reassess the relationships between modern birds.

topics.title: Telluraves
topics.text: Telluraves, also called land birds, are a group of birds that live in trees. Scientists recently grouped them using new genetic studies.

topics.title: Tinamou
topics.text: A tinamou is one of an family of birds called the Tinamidae. They are the only species within the family.

topics.title: Tropicbird
topics.text: Tropicbirds are pelagic seabirds that occur in tropical areas and seas of the world. There are three living species.

topics.title: Turaco
topics.text: The turacos make up the bird family Musophagidae ( "banana-eaters"), which includes plantain-eaters and go-away-birds. In southern Africa both turacos and go-away-birds are commonly known as loeries.

topics.title: Water bird
topics.text: A water bird is one who lives on or around water. It includes water fowl, sea birds, wading birds and shore birds.
